summary: Defines an abstract model for a presence and instant messaging system, including the entities involved, the terminology, and the services provided. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2778 defines shared terms for systems that publish presence information and deliver instant messages. The model helps people describe and compare these systems, but it does not specify a protocol or require a particular design.

subtitle: A shared vocabulary for the parts and services in presence and instant messaging systems.

tldr.problem: People needed common terms for discussing systems that share presence information and deliver instant messages.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an abstract model of two services, their clients, the information they handle, and the protocols that connect them.
tldr.outcome: It is a descriptive model, not an implementation plan or an interoperability specification.

today: RFC 2778 is Informational, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The document defines an abstract model and vocabulary for presence and instant messaging systems.

sections.title: Purpose and Limits of the Model
sections.content:
Presence systems let users request information about one another and learn when it changes. Instant messaging systems let users send short messages. RFC 2778 names the entities and services involved so later work can discuss requirements with shared terms.

The model is intended to describe a broad range of systems. It is not prescriptive and does not define interoperable protocols. An entity in the model may be combined with other entities or may not exist as a separate part in an implementation. The RFC writes model terms in uppercase.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives people shared names for the parts of presence and messaging systems. It describes possible roles, but does not require software to build each role as a separate component.

sections.title: The Presence Service and Its Clients
sections.content:
The PRESENCE SERVICE accepts, stores, and distributes PRESENCE INFORMATION. PRESENTITIES provide that information, and WATCHERS request or receive it. A FETCHER asks for the current information. A POLLER is a fetcher that repeats the request regularly. A SUBSCRIBER asks to be notified of future changes.

The service may also keep WATCHER INFORMATION about who has requested presence information and may share it with some watchers. A PRESENCE PROTOCOL carries exchanges between the service, presentities, and watchers. The RFC does not define the protocol's message format.
sections.plainLanguage: A presentity provides information about its presence. A watcher can ask for the current information or subscribe to receive notices when it changes.

sections.title: The Instant Message Service
sections.content:
The INSTANT MESSAGE SERVICE accepts and delivers INSTANT MESSAGES. SENDERS provide messages to the service. Each message names an INSTANT INBOX ADDRESS, and the service attempts to deliver it to the matching INSTANT INBOX.

The RFC describes an instant message as an identifiable, small unit of data, but deliberately does not define a size. The service may use servers or proxies, may have different authentication requirements, or may connect a sender directly to an inbox. The model leaves these choices open.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender gives a message and an inbox address to the instant message service. The service tries to deliver that message to the matching inbox.

sections.title: Presence Information and Status
sections.content:
PRESENCE INFORMATION contains one or more PRESENCE TUPLES. Each tuple has a STATUS, an optional COMMUNICATION ADDRESS, and optional OTHER PRESENCE MARKUP. A communication address pairs a communication method with a contact address.

The model defines OPEN and CLOSED as status values that affect instant messages. OPEN means the associated inbox can accept a message; CLOSED means it cannot. Other status values may be meaningful to software or people, and the model allows status to contain one or several values.
sections.plainLanguage: Presence information can contain a status and an optional way to contact someone. OPEN means the inbox can accept an instant message; CLOSED means it cannot.

sections.title: Principals and User Agents
sections.content:
A PRINCIPAL is a person, group, or program that the system treats as one distinct actor. The model does not define how real people or organizations map to principals. A principal uses the system through user agents that connect it to a presentity, watcher, sender, or inbox.

The model separates these user-agent roles even though an implementation may combine them. The RFC's examples describe a buddy list as presence and watcher user agents, and an instant messenger as those roles combined with sender and inbox user agents.
sections.plainLanguage: A principal is the person, group, or program the system treats as one actor. User agents connect that actor to the system, and one application may perform several user-agent roles.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three security problems: STALKING, SPOOFING, and SPAM. Stalking uses presence information to infer someone's whereabouts for malicious or illegal purposes. Spoofing is one principal improperly imitating another. Spam is unwanted instant messages.

The model associates access rules, visibility rules, and watcher information with addressing stalking; authentication with addressing spoofing; and delivery rules with addressing spam. These are parts of the model, not detailed security mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC names three risks: misuse of presence information, pretending to be another user, and unwanted messages. It identifies model features that can address these risks, but does not define their implementation.
